summary: This video presents a hands-on Photoshop workflow for high-dynamic-range landscape work in Alaska—centered on ice-cave imagery and glacier scenery. The speaker advocates starting from a blank canvas to sculpt light, uses focus stacking with RAW data, and demonstrates careful sky replacement and color grading across multiple exposures. Key techniques include maintaining tripod stability for stacking, pre-stack dynamic-range extraction, auto-align/auto-blend of layers, texture-driven adjustments, fog and atmosphere via Orton-style diffusion, blue-luminance separation to texture layers, and a simulated light source to guide the viewer’s eye. Throughout, the presenter emphasizes composition (rule of odds, leading lines), practical considerations (camera movement, card speed, and file formats), and the iterative nature of editing as an undoing-and-rebuilding process rather than a single linear sequence.

sections.title: Gear context and optical setup for ice-cave shots
concepts: 10 mm lens for wide, cathedral-like cave geometry
sections.description: Introduces the practical impact of using a very wide lens (10 mm) on ice-cave shots and how it helps bend ceiling lines toward a strong foreground. Sets the stage for the emphasis on strong lines, minimal flare, and foreground dominance.

sections.title: Philosophy of processing as an undoing journey
concepts: blank canvas approach to light shaping
sections.description: Articulates a processing philosophy: start by removing excess light and contrast to rebuild light flow intentionally, emphasizing that effective tonal control comes from the ability to re-create light rather than simply adjusting existing tones.

sections.title: Tripod discipline and stack readiness
concepts: avoidance of movement for stacking results
sections.description: Highlights tripod discipline as essential for reliable stacking and exposure blending. Warns that even slight movement ruins focus stacking and exposure alignments.

sections.title: Initial RAW processing and stack assembly
concepts: texture/clarity/saturation warmth adjustments prior to stacking
sections.description: Describes loading frames into a Photoshop stack, applying initial global adjustments, and performing RAW-range extraction before stacking to preserve maximum dynamic range.

sections.title: Focus stack scale and multi-shot composition awareness
concepts: large stacks (30 frames) vs smaller sets
sections.description: Discusses the scale of focus stacks and evaluates when a large 30-shot stack may be overkill, stressing the importance of cleaner, more controlled stacks.

sections.title: Sky blending fundamentals and horizon handling
sections.description: Details the process of blending skies from multiple exposures, including matching color temperature and ensuring the horizon line is not directly touched to prevent seams and color mismatches.

sections.title: Horizon alignment and horizon-safe masking
sections.description: Emphasizes protecting the horizon during sky blending and using inverse selections to prevent artifacts at the seam line.

sections.title: Color, tonal, and luminosity layering across sky and mountains
sections.description: Introduces a repeatable color-tonal workflow to pull out mountain light, expand color separation across layers, and apply targeted color grading to preserve realism while enhancing dramatic lighting.

sections.title: Layer alignment and content-aware stacking
sections.description: Demonstrates Photoshop’s automatic alignment and content-aware fill for seamless composites, noting how properly separated layers stack cleanly with minimal masking.

sections.title: Perspective changes and foreground cleanups
concepts: field-captured multiple angles to reduce obstructions
sections.description: Discusses removing intrusive foreground elements (like a stick) by shifting perspective and taking multiple shots to blend later.

sections.title: Fog diffusion and blue-luminance separation for layering
sections.description: Shows diffusion-based softening (Orton effect) and blue-luminance separation to create layered fog that adds depth without destroying underlying textures.

sections.title: Simulated light source and atmospheric finishing touches
sections.description: Introduces a simulated light source technique using diffusion and luminosity to guide viewer focus, followed by layered color grading to unify sky and foreground lighting.
